context.heading: Three sins, even four
context.body: "For three transgressions, even four" is a Hebrew counting pattern also found in Proverbs 30. It does not mean a nation committed exactly four crimes. It means sin piled on sin until the cup overflowed, and the one crime Amos then names is the final straw.

context.heading: Threshing people like grain
context.body: Dush ("threshed") describes dragging a heavy wooden sledge, studded with sharp iron or stone, over harvested grain. Aram did this to the people of Gilead. Second Kings 13:7 uses similar language: the king of Aram made Israel's army "like the dust at threshing."

context.heading: The earthquake everyone remembered
context.body: Ra'ash ("earthquake") dates Amos's preaching to two years before a quake so severe it became a reference point, like "before the war." Excavations at Hazor and other northern sites show earthquake damage from around the mid 700s BC, and Zechariah 14:5 still recalls it centuries later.

theology.title: Judge of every nation
theology.body: Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon and Moab never received the Law at Sinai, yet God holds them guilty for atrocities: selling whole villages as slaves, breaking treaties, brutality against the defenseless. Paul makes the same point in Romans 2:14–15. Every person bears God's image and knows cruelty is wrong.

theology.title: The roar from Zion
theology.body: Amos opens with God roaring from Zion and Jerusalem (v. 2), the same words as Joel 3:16. Amos is preaching in the north, where Israel worshiped at Bethel and Dan. His first line reminds them where God had chosen to place His name.

application.title: Cheering for judgment
application.body: Amos's audience would have applauded as each enemy was condemned. Then the circle closed on them. It is easy to agree that God should judge other people.
application.question: Whose sins are you quick to condemn while your own go unexamined?

application.title: No one is exempt
application.body: These nations had no Bible, yet God judged their cruelty. Ignorance of Scripture does not excuse treating people like objects.
application.question: Where do you see people treated as disposable in your workplace or community, and what could you do about it?

application.title: Broken covenants
application.body: Tyre is condemned for forgetting "a covenant of brotherhood" (v. 9). God takes broken promises between people seriously.
application.question: What promise to a friend, spouse or colleague have you quietly let lapse?

context.heading: The cloak by the altar
context.body: Chaval ("taken in pledge") means to seize something as collateral. The Law said a poor person's cloak, often his only blanket, must be returned by nightfall (Exodus 22:26–27). Israel's elite instead lounged on those cloaks beside the altar, turning a worship feast into a display of what they had taken.

context.heading: Judah's charge is different
context.body: The nations were condemned for cruelty; Judah is condemned because they rejected the torah ("Law") of the LORD. Torah means instruction, the guidance of a father to a child. Judah had more light than its neighbors, so its guilt was measured by what it had received.

context.heading: Exploiting the vulnerable
context.body: A father and son both using "the same girl" (v. 7) most likely describes a servant girl in the household who had no power to refuse. Some think it refers to ritual prostitution. Either way, God names sexual exploitation of the vulnerable as a profanation of His holy name.

theology.title: The God who remembers His grace
theology.body: Verses 9–11 interrupt the accusations with God's own memories: He destroyed the Amorites, brought Israel out of Egypt, led them forty years and raised up prophets. Israel's sin is not just law breaking; it is ingratitude toward a Redeemer who gave them everything.

theology.title: He hears the poor
theology.body: Exodus 22:27 says that when the poor man without his cloak cries out, "I will hear, for I am compassionate." Amos shows that promise in action. The God of Israel takes the side of people who have no one else to defend them (Psalm 146:7–9).

application.title: Sunday and Monday
application.body: Israel worshiped beside the altar using goods squeezed from the poor. Faith that ignores how we treat people in business is not the faith God accepts.
application.question: What part of how you earn or spend money would you be uncomfortable bringing to church with you?

application.title: Silencing the voices
application.body: Israel told prophets to stop prophesying and pressured Nazirites to break their vows (v. 12). We can do the same by mocking or sidelining people whose faithfulness makes us uneasy.
application.question: Whose example of faithfulness do you find yourself quietly discouraging?

application.title: Strength will not save you
application.body: Verses 14–16 list the swift, the strong and the skilled archer, and none escape. Talent and resources are no protection against God.
application.question: What personal strength are you counting on to keep you safe from consequences?

context.heading: What the shepherd brings back
context.body: Exodus 22:13 let a shepherd prove a lion had killed a sheep by bringing back the remains. So a "rescue" of two legs or a piece of an ear is not good news; it is evidence that the animal is dead. Samaria's survivors will be like scraps of furniture left after a disaster.

context.heading: Foreign witnesses called in
context.body: God summons the strongholds of Ashdod and Egypt to gather on Samaria's hills and watch (v. 9). Philistines and Egyptians were Israel's old oppressors. The point is shaming: even pagan nations would be appalled at the cruelty and plunder inside Israel's capital.

context.heading: Horns of the altar
context.body: Altars had horn shaped corners, and a fugitive could grab them to seek protection (1 Kings 1:50). Cutting off Bethel's altar horns means there will be no sanctuary to run to when judgment comes.

theology.title: Privilege means responsibility
theology.body: "Only you have I known... therefore I will punish you" (v. 2). Israel thought being chosen meant immunity. Amos says it means accountability. Jesus says the same: "From everyone who has been given much, much will be required" (Luke 12:48).

theology.title: God speaks before He acts
theology.body: God does nothing without revealing His plan to His prophets (v. 7), as He told Abraham before judging Sodom (Genesis 18:17). His warnings are a mercy. Hebrews 1:1–2 says that in these last days He has spoken fully through His Son.

application.title: Walking together
application.body: "Do two walk together unless they have agreed?" (v. 3). Closeness with God is not automatic; it depends on going the same direction.
application.question: In what area of life are you asking God to walk with you while refusing to go His way?

application.title: They do not know how to do right
application.body: Verse 10 says Samaria's elite stored up plunder until they lost the ability to tell right from wrong. Habits of small injustice slowly blind us.
application.question: What compromise have you repeated so often that it no longer feels wrong?

application.title: Two homes, no peace
application.body: Winter houses and summer houses (v. 15) were the dream of the day. Comfort can become the thing we serve instead of a gift we use.
application.question: What would you be most afraid to lose if God tested where your security really lies?

context.heading: Tithes every three days
context.body: The Law asked for a special tithe every three years (Deuteronomy 14:28). Amos sarcastically tells Israel to bring tithes every three days. Their worship was enthusiastic and frequent, and they loved announcing their freewill offerings (v. 5), but it was all about being seen.

context.heading: Five times: you did not return
context.body: Shuv ("return") is the Old Testament's main word for repentance, turning around. Five times God lists a disaster He sent and repeats the refrain, "yet you did not return to Me." Each echoes a covenant warning from Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. The hardships were alarms that went unheard.

context.heading: A burning stick
context.body: "A firebrand snatched from the fire" (v. 11) is a half burnt stick pulled out just in time. Zechariah 3:2 uses the same image of the high priest Joshua. Israel had been rescued from disaster before, and still had not changed.

theology.title: Discipline as mercy
theology.body: The famine, drought and plague were not random. God sent them to bring His people home. Hebrews 12:5–11 says the Lord disciplines those He loves. Hardship is not always punishment, but God can use any hardship to call us back.

theology.title: The God who forms mountains
theology.body: Verse 13 is a hymn: God forms the mountains, creates the wind, reveals His thoughts to people and treads the heights of the earth. The God Israel must meet is not a local shrine deity but the Creator of everything. That makes the meeting both terrifying and hopeful.

application.title: Generosity for an audience
application.body: Israel loved to publicize its offerings (v. 5). Jesus warned against giving "to be seen by others" (Matthew 6:1–4).
application.question: How much of your giving would continue if nobody, not even your spouse or friends, ever knew about it?

application.title: Reading the alarms
application.body: God repeated the same message five times through hard events. We can explain every setback away without ever asking what God might be saying.
application.question: What recurring difficulty in your life might be an invitation to turn rather than just a problem to fix?

application.title: Prepare to meet
application.body: Every person will one day stand before God (v. 12; Hebrews 9:27). Preparation is not a feeling but a turning, done now.
application.question: If you met God tomorrow, what would you most wish you had already dealt with?

context.heading: Justice in the gate
context.body: The city gate was where elders sat to hear cases, settle land deals and witness contracts (Ruth 4:1–11). Sha'ar ("gate") is the setting of Israel's courts. When Amos says "establish justice in the gate," he means fix the courtroom, where bribes were pushing aside the poor (v. 12).

context.heading: Rejected, not abolished
context.body: Ma'as ("despise") is strong: to reject, to refuse. Yet God Himself had commanded these feasts (Leviticus 23). He is not rejecting worship itself but worship that comes from hands stained by injustice. Isaiah 1:11–17, Hosea 6:6 and Psalm 51:16–19 make the same point.

context.heading: Darkness, not light
context.body: Israel longed for "the Day of the LORD," expecting God to defeat their enemies. Amos turns the expectation upside down: for a sinful Israel it will be like escaping a lion only to meet a bear, then being bitten by a snake at home (vv. 18–20).

theology.title: Seek Me, not a place
theology.body: "Seek Me and live" (v. 4), not Bethel, Gilgal or Beersheba. God refuses to be reduced to a shrine people visit. Jesus told the Samaritan woman that true worshipers worship in spirit and truth, not on a particular mountain (John 4:21–24).

theology.title: Worship and justice belong together
theology.body: Amos is not choosing ethics over worship. He insists they cannot be separated. Jesus tells us to be reconciled with a brother before offering a gift (Matthew 5:23–24), and James calls pure religion caring for orphans and widows (James 1:27).

theology.title: Quoted by Stephen
theology.body: Verses 25–27 recall Israel's idolatry back in the wilderness. Stephen quotes them from the Greek Old Testament in Acts 7:42–43 to show that God's people had long resisted Him. Amos's warning became part of the church's earliest preaching.

application.title: Hating the messenger
application.body: Verse 10 describes people who hate whoever tells the truth in court. We rarely resent lies as much as we resent being corrected.
application.question: Who has told you an honest truth recently that you have been avoiding ever since?

application.title: Justice where you sit
application.body: Few of us run a court, but many of us decide things: hiring, pricing, grading, who gets a second chance. Amos's justice starts in those places.
application.question: Where in your daily decisions do you have the power to treat someone more fairly this week?

application.title: Turn off the noise
application.body: God tells Israel to take away the noise of their songs (v. 23). Beautiful worship can become a way of drowning out what God is actually saying.
application.question: What part of your spiritual routine might be keeping you busy instead of keeping you listening?

context.heading: Not grieved over the ruin
context.body: Shever ("ruin") means a breaking, a fracture, like a broken bone. Joseph, the father of the northern tribes, stands for the whole nation. Israel's leaders could see the cracks in their society, but they did not feel them. The problem was not ignorance but indifference.

context.heading: Rejoicing over nothing
context.body: Lo debar means "nothing," and Karnaim means "horns," a symbol of strength. Both were towns Jeroboam II recaptured (2 Kings 14:25). Amos mocks Israel for celebrating a victory over "Nothing" and boasting that they took "Horns" by their own strength (v. 13).

context.heading: Do not say the Name
context.body: Verses 9–10 picture a house where everyone has died and a relative comes to burn the bodies. When asked about survivors he says, "Hush, we must not mention the name of the LORD." The people who once invoked God casually now fear that even saying His name will bring more judgment.

theology.title: God hates pride
theology.body: "I abhor the pride of Jacob" (v. 8). The word for pride, ga'on, can mean majesty, but here it is self glory. God swears by Himself, as there is no one greater to swear by (Hebrews 6:13). Pride is not a minor flaw; it puts us in God's place.

theology.title: Justice turned to poison
theology.body: Horses do not run on cliffs, and no one plows the sea with oxen (v. 12). Turning justice into poison is just as unnatural. Sin is not only forbidden; it goes against the grain of the world God made.

application.title: Comfortable and numb
application.body: The problem in Samaria was not wine or music but people enjoying both while ignoring a breaking nation. Comfort becomes sin when it makes us stop caring.
application.question: What hard news do you scroll past because it would interrupt your comfort?

application.title: Songs like David
application.body: Verse 5 says they improvised music like David. David's songs included laments; theirs were for parties only.
application.question: When was the last time you grieved before God over something broken in your church or community?

application.title: Small wins, big boasts
application.body: Israel celebrated taking Lo debar, "Nothing," as proof of its strength. We can inflate small successes into reasons to feel secure.
application.question: What achievement are you leaning on that God might call Lo debar?

context.heading: Treason at the royal chapel
context.body: Qashar ("conspired") is the word used for plots to overthrow kings, and Israel had seen several (2 Kings 15:10). By calling Amos a conspirator, the priest Amaziah turned a religious message into a political crime, a familiar way to silence unwelcome voices.

context.heading: The king's sanctuary
context.body: Amaziah calls Bethel the miqdash ("sanctuary") of the king and the temple of the kingdom (v. 13). The shrine existed to support the throne. In his mind, a prophet who threatened the king had no right to speak there, whatever God said.

context.heading: The king's mowing
context.body: The first vision mentions locusts arriving after "the king's mowing" (v. 1). The first cut of spring grass probably went to the royal stables as tax. The locusts would strike the second crop, the one ordinary farmers depended on to get through the dry summer.

theology.title: God listens to intercession
theology.body: Twice Amos cries, "How can Jacob survive? He is so small!" and twice the LORD relents (vv. 2–6). Like Abraham (Genesis 18) and Moses (Exodus 32:11–14), Amos shows that prayer for others matters to God. Only at the plumb line does God say He will spare them no longer.

theology.title: The God who calls ordinary people
theology.body: "The LORD took me from following the flock" (v. 15) echoes God's words to David (2 Samuel 7:8). God chooses messengers without credentials, as Jesus called fishermen. Authority comes from His call, not from a guild or a title.

application.title: Pray for the small
application.body: Amos did not argue that Israel deserved mercy; he appealed to how small and weak it was. That is a prayer anyone can pray for people they love.
application.question: Who in your life is too weak to stand on their own, and when did you last plead with God for them by name?

application.title: When truth sounds disloyal
application.body: Amaziah framed honest preaching as an attack on the nation. People still label uncomfortable truth as disloyalty to the group.
application.question: When have you dismissed a hard word because of whose side the speaker seemed to be on?

application.title: No credentials required
application.body: Amos had no title, just a call. Many people hold back from serving because they feel unqualified.
application.question: What has God put in front of you that you keep postponing until you feel qualified?

context.heading: Shrinking the measure
context.body: Merchants made the ephah, the dry measure for grain, smaller and the shekel weight heavier. Customers got less grain and paid more silver. Mirmah ("dishonest") means deceit, built into the scales themselves. Deuteronomy 25:13–16 calls dishonest weights detestable to God.

context.heading: Waiting for the Sabbath to end
context.body: The New Moon and Sabbath were days of rest when markets closed. These merchants kept the rules outwardly while counting the hours until they could reopen. The Sabbath, God's gift of rest, had become an obstacle to profit.

context.heading: Sun down at noon
context.body: Verse 9 pictures the sun setting at midday. A total solar eclipse was visible in the region on June 15, 763 BC, recorded in Assyrian records. Many scholars think Amos's hearers would have remembered it, though the verse may simply be a picture of judgment.

theology.title: God does not forget
theology.body: "I will never forget any of their deeds" (v. 7). People may think small frauds vanish in the ledger. The God who sees the widow's mite (Mark 12:41–44) also sees the shrunken measure.

theology.title: A famine of the word
theology.body: God's word is life: "man does not live on bread alone" (Deuteronomy 8:3), which Jesus quotes in Matthew 4:4. The worst judgment Amos describes is not hunger but God's silence. Those who rejected His prophets would one day stagger from sea to sea looking for a word and not find it (v. 12).

application.title: Honest scales today
application.body: Hidden fees, padded invoices, shrinking packages and cut corners are modern false measures. God cares about the fine print.
application.question: Where in your work could a customer or employer be getting less than they think they are paying for?

application.title: Resenting rest
application.body: These merchants treated the Sabbath as lost income. Many of us treat rest the same way, always half on the clock.
application.question: What would it cost you to stop working completely for one day a week, and what does that cost reveal?

application.title: Bread you are not eating
application.body: Amos warns of a day when God's word would be hard to find. Many of us carry Scripture on our phones and still go hungry.
application.question: What gets more of your attention each morning than the word of God?

context.heading: Like the Cushites
context.body: God asks whether Israel is any different to Him than the Kushi ("Cushites"), the distant people of the upper Nile. He also brought the Philistines from Caphtor (probably Crete) and the Arameans from Kir. Israel's exodus was real, but it did not make them immune; God directs every nation's history.

context.heading: Nowhere to hide
context.body: Sheol, the realm of the dead, was the deepest place imaginable; heaven the highest. Verses 2–4 list every hiding place, even the sea floor and captivity, and God is there. Psalm 139:7–12 uses the same picture for comfort; here it is a warning.

context.heading: Edom or mankind
context.body: Verse 12 speaks of Israel possessing "the remnant of Edom." The Greek translation, which James quotes in Acts 15:17, reads "the rest of mankind." In Hebrew, Edom and adam ("mankind") differ by one small letter. Either way, the nations are brought under the rule of David's restored house.

theology.title: David's house rebuilt in Christ
theology.body: At the Jerusalem council James quotes verses 11–12 to show that Gentiles coming to faith fulfill this promise (Acts 15:15–18). Jesus, the Son of David, is raising the fallen house, and its reach now includes the nations. Christians differ on whether verses 14–15 also promise a future return of ethnic Israel to the land.

theology.title: Judgment that sifts
theology.body: God shakes Israel among the nations like grain in a sieve (v. 9). The image is debated: does it catch every sinner, or keep every grain safe? Either way, God's judgment is not blind destruction. He knows each person, and verse 8 promises He will not wipe out the house of Jacob entirely.

application.title: Identity is not immunity
application.body: Israel thought its history guaranteed safety. Church membership, a Christian family or a past decision can become the same false security.
application.question: What part of your religious background are you treating as a guarantee instead of a gift?

application.title: Hope after ruin
application.body: Amos ends with vineyards replanted and cities rebuilt. God's last word to His people is restoration, not rubble.
application.question: What area of your life feels like a fallen booth that you need to hand back to God to rebuild?

application.title: No hiding places
application.body: We hide from God in busyness, entertainment or simply not praying. Amos says there is nowhere He is not.
application.question: Where are you currently trying to keep God at a distance, and why?
